Categorical summary tables

Source: vignettes/articles/table-categorical.Rmd
table-categorical.Rmd
library(spicy)

table_categorical() builds publication-ready categorical tables for reports and articles in social science and data science research. With by, it produces grouped cross-tabulation tables with \(p\)-values from the chi-squared or Fisher’s exact test, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and multi-level headers. Without by, it produces one-way frequency-style tables for the selected variables. Export to gt, tinytable, flextable, Excel, or Word. Formatting follows APA conventions by default; style = "jama" (or "nejm", "lancet", "annals", "aer") switches the whole table to that journal’s published rules — the House styles section of Summary tables for reporting shows each style and the guideline sentence behind every rule. This article walks through the main features.

Basic usage

For grouped tables, provide a data frame, one or more selected variables, and a grouping variable:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity, dentist_12m),
  by = education
)
#> Categorical table by education
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Lower secondary n  Lower secondary %  Upper secondary n 
#> ───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking           │                                                         
#>    No              │        179               69.6                415        
#>    Yes             │         78               30.4                112        
#>    (Missing)       │          4                                    12        
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  physical_activity │                                                         
#>    No              │        177               67.8                310        
#>    Yes             │         84               32.2                229        
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  dentist_12m       │                                                         
#>    No              │        113               43.3                174        
#>    Yes             │        148               56.7                365        
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Upper secondary %  Tertiary n  Tertiary %  Total n 
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking           │                                                    
#>    No              │       78.7            332         84.9       926   
#>    Yes             │       21.3             59         15.1       249   
#>    (Missing)       │                         9                     25   
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  physical_activity │                                                    
#>    No              │       57.5            163         40.8       650   
#>    Yes             │       42.5            237         59.2       550   
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  dentist_12m       │                                                    
#>    No              │       32.3             67         16.8       354   
#>    Yes             │       67.7            333         83.2       846   
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Total %    p     V  
#> ───────────────────┼─────────────────────
#>  smoking           │          <.001  .14 
#>    No              │  78.8               
#>    Yes             │  21.2               
#>    (Missing)       │                     
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  physical_activity │          <.001  .21 
#>    No              │  54.2               
#>    Yes             │  45.8               
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  dentist_12m       │          <.001  .22 
#>    No              │  29.5               
#>    Yes             │  70.5               
#> 
#> Note. N = 1200: Lower secondary (n = 261), Upper secondary (n = 539), Tertiary (n = 400). Percentages are column percentages. P-values: Pearson chi-squared test. V = Cramér's V.

The default output is "default", which prints a styled ASCII table to the console, folded into successive panels when it is wider than the console. Reading the table: each level of by gets a pair of columns, the count n and the column percentage computed within that group – percentages sum to 100 down each education group (for smoking within “Lower secondary”: 69.6 + 30.4 = 100.0, the four missing answers counted in their own row, out of the base) – and the Total pair is the margin over all groups combined. The note opens with the sample size and the size of each group, then says the direction of the percentages. In the last panel, p is the p-value of the test of association between the row variable and by, computed once per variable on its full cross-table (Pearson’s chi-squared here, as the note says; see the test section below), and the final column is the association measure – here Cramér’s V (covered below). Use output = "data.frame" for a plain data frame suitable for further processing.

percent = "row" reads the table the other way: each cell is the share of the row’s respondents that falls in the group, so the percentages sum to 100 across each row and the Total column shows 100. total_row = TRUE closes the block with a Total row, the share of each group overall, the base rate the rows are compared with. With smoking as by, 29.9% of the respondents with lower secondary education smoke and 14.8% of those with tertiary education, against 20.8% overall. Only the percentages change: the counts, the test and the association measure are those of the column direction, and the note says the percentages are row percentages.

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = education,
  by = smoking,
  percent = "row",
  total_row = TRUE
)
#> Categorical table by smoking
#> 
#>  Variable          │ No n  No %  Yes n  Yes %  (Missing) n  (Missing) % 
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  education         │                                                    
#>    Lower secondary │ 179   68.6    78   29.9        4           1.5     
#>    Upper secondary │ 415   77.0   112   20.8       12           2.2     
#>    Tertiary        │ 332   83.0    59   14.8        9           2.2     
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>    Total           │ 926   77.2   249   20.8       25           2.1     
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Total n  Total %    p     V  
#> ───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────
#>  education         │                   <.001  .14 
#>    Lower secondary │   261     100.0              
#>    Upper secondary │   539     100.0              
#>    Tertiary        │   400     100.0              
#> ───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────
#>    Total           │  1200     100.0              
#> 
#> Note. N = 1200: No (n = 926), Yes (n = 249), (Missing) (n = 25). Percentages are row percentages. P-value: Pearson chi-squared test. V = Cramér's V.

One-way tables

Omit by to build a frequency-style table for the selected variables:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity)
)
#> Categorical table
#> 
#>  Variable            │   n      %    
#> ─────────────────────┼───────────────
#>  smoking             │               
#>    No                │  926    78.8  
#>    Yes               │  249    21.2  
#>    (Missing)         │   25          
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  physical_activity   │               
#>    No                │  650    54.2  
#>    Yes               │  550    45.8  
#> 
#> Note. N = 1200.

select itself is optional: when omitted, the table includes every eligible categorical column in the data – factor, character, logical, and labelled (haven) columns – excluding the by column, mirroring the select-less defaults of table_continuous() and table_continuous_lm(). An explicit select is taken verbatim, so numeric-coded categorical variables can still be tabulated by naming them.

Output formats

table_categorical() supports several output formats. The table below summarizes the options:

Format Description
"default" Styled ASCII table in the console (default)
"data.frame" The displayed table, with its numbers
"long" Long data frame, one row per level x group
"gt" Formatted gt table
"tinytable" Formatted tinytable
"flextable" Formatted flextable
"excel" Excel file (requires excel_path)
"clipboard" Copy to clipboard
"word" Word document (requires word_path)

The three rendered formats ("gt", "tinytable", "flextable") are demonstrated in the final section, together with the file exports.

Data frame output

Use output = "data.frame" for the table as it is displayed, with its numbers: one row per printed row, the key columns variable (the column name), label, level and .row_role ("factor_header" for the row of a variable, which carries its p-value and association measure, "level", or "missing" for the row of missing values), then the counts, the full-precision percentages, p and the measure under the names the table prints. as.data.frame() on the printed table returns the same frame:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = smoking,
  by = education,
  output = "data.frame"
)
#>   variable   label     level     .row_role Lower secondary n Lower secondary %
#> 1  smoking smoking      <NA> factor_header                NA                NA
#> 2  smoking smoking        No         level               179          69.64981
#> 3  smoking smoking       Yes         level                78          30.35019
#> 4  smoking smoking (Missing)       missing                 4                NA
#>   Upper secondary n Upper secondary % Tertiary n Tertiary % Total n  Total %
#> 1                NA                NA         NA         NA      NA       NA
#> 2               415          78.74763        332   84.91049     926 78.80851
#> 3               112          21.25237         59   15.08951     249 21.19149
#> 4                12                NA          9         NA      25       NA
#>              p         V
#> 1 2.012877e-05 0.1356677
#> 2           NA        NA
#> 3           NA        NA
#> 4           NA        NA

Use output = "long" for one row per level and group, the Total margin included and flagged by total, with the test of each variable (test_type, statistic, df, p.value) and its association measure (es_type, es_value) on every row of its block:

head(table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = smoking,
  by = education,
  output = "long"
), 4)
#>   variable   label level .row_role           group .group_role total   n
#> 1  smoking smoking    No     level Lower secondary       group FALSE 179
#> 2  smoking smoking    No     level Upper secondary       group FALSE 415
#> 3  smoking smoking    No     level        Tertiary       group FALSE 332
#> 4  smoking smoking    No     level           Total       total  TRUE 926
#>        pct   test_type statistic df      p.value  es_type  es_value es_ci_lower
#> 1 69.64981 chi_squared  21.62672  2 2.012877e-05 cramer_v 0.1356677          NA
#> 2 78.74763 chi_squared  21.62672  2 2.012877e-05 cramer_v 0.1356677          NA
#> 3 84.91049 chi_squared  21.62672  2 2.012877e-05 cramer_v 0.1356677          NA
#> 4 78.80851 chi_squared  21.62672  2 2.012877e-05 cramer_v 0.1356677          NA
#>   es_ci_upper smd_type smd_value
#> 1          NA     <NA>        NA
#> 2          NA     <NA>        NA
#> 3          NA     <NA>        NA
#> 4          NA     <NA>        NA

Custom labels

By default, table_categorical() labels each row block with the column name. labels = TRUE uses the variable’s label attribute when one is present (e.g. data imported with haven), and the column name otherwise. A named character vector keyed by column name sets the labels you publish: the listed columns take them, and the others follow options(spicy.var_labels) (their name unless it is TRUE). labels = var_labels(smoking = "Smoking status") renames the same way while the others keep their label attribute. A name that matches no column of the table warns and is left out, so one vector can still serve every table of a report (wrap the call in suppressWarnings() to quiet it). The by variable in the title follows the same rule, as in the other summary tables. (Unnamed positional label vectors, accepted before 0.13.0, now raise an error.)

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
  by = education,
  labels = c(
    smoking           = "Smoking status",
    physical_activity = "Regular physical activity"
  )
)
#> Categorical table by education
#> 
#>  Variable                  │ Lower secondary n  Lower secondary % 
#> ───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────
#>  Smoking status            │                                      
#>    No                      │        179               69.6        
#>    Yes                     │         78               30.4        
#>    (Missing)               │          4                           
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌

#> ───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────

Association measures and confidence intervals

table_categorical() picks the association measure per row variable based on the variable type (assoc_measure = "auto", the default):

  • 2x2 (binary row variable vs. binary by) -> phi,
  • both ordered factors -> Kendall’s tau_b,
  • otherwise -> Cramér’s V.

A measure used for every row heads the column, and names it in the data frames, with its symbol (V for Cramér’s V, φ for phi, τb for Kendall’s tau-b, γ for gamma; the other measures keep their names). The note defines the symbol as it defines any abbreviation: V by default, the Greek letters under spicy_style(abbreviations = "all"). When the chosen measures differ across rows, the column header collapses to "Effect size" and the table note names the measure used for each variable.

Seven measures are available: "cramer_v", "phi", "gamma", "tau_b", "tau_c", "somers_d", and "lambda"; assoc_measure = "none" drops the column entirely. See ?table_categorical for the dispatch details and Cramér’s V, Phi, and association measures for definitions and guidance on choosing among them. Override the automatic choice with a single string for uniform application, or with a named vector to mix measures per row:

# Uniform: same measure for every row variable
table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = smoking,
  by = education,
  assoc_measure = "lambda"
)
#> Categorical table by education
#> 
#>  Variable    │ Lower secondary n  Lower secondary %  Upper secondary n 
#> ─────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking     │                                                         
#>    No        │        179               69.6                415        
#>    Yes       │         78               30.4                112        
#>    (Missing) │          4                                    12        
#> 
#>  Variable    │ Upper secondary %  Tertiary n  Tertiary %  Total n  Total % 
#> ─────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking     │                                                             
#>    No        │       78.7            332         84.9       926     78.8   
#>    Yes       │       21.3             59         15.1       249     21.2   
#>    (Missing) │                         9                     25            
#> 
#>  Variable    │   p    Lambda 
#> ─────────────┼───────────────
#>  smoking     │ <.001   .00   
#>    No        │               
#>    Yes       │               
#>    (Missing) │               
#> 
#> Note. N = 1200: Lower secondary (n = 261), Upper secondary (n = 539), Tertiary (n = 400). Percentages are column percentages. P-value: Pearson chi-squared test.

A significant chi-squared p-value next to a lambda of exactly .00 is not a contradiction. Goodman-Kruskal lambda measures the proportional reduction in the error of predicting the row variable once the group is known, and it is exactly 0 whenever the modal category is the same in every group: here “No” is the most frequent answer at all three education levels (68.6%, 77.0%, 83.0%), so knowing education never changes the best single guess, even though the distributions clearly differ (hence the significant chi-squared test).

In a named vector, variables you do not name keep the "auto" choice, so only the overrides need to be listed. Here "auto" would pick Cramér’s V for smoking (binary x ordered, not 2x2) and Kendall’s Tau-b for self_rated_health (ordered x ordered); the named vector keeps the former and replaces the latter with Goodman-Kruskal Gamma:

# Named vector: override "auto" for one variable only
table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, self_rated_health),
  by = education,
  assoc_measure = c(self_rated_health = "gamma")
)
#> Categorical table by education
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Lower secondary n  Lower secondary %  Upper secondary n 
#> ───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking           │                                                         
#>    No              │        179               69.6                415        
#>    Yes             │         78               30.4                112        
#>    (Missing)       │          4                                    12        
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  self_rated_health │                                                         
#>    Poor            │         28               10.8                 28        
#>    Fair            │         86               33.1                118        
#>    Good            │        102               39.2                263        
#>    Very good       │         44               16.9                118        
#>    (Missing)       │          1                                    12        
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Upper secondary %  Tertiary n  Tertiary %  Total n 
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking           │                                                    
#>    No              │       78.7            332         84.9       926   
#>    Yes             │       21.3             59         15.1       249   
#>    (Missing)       │                         9                     25   
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  self_rated_health │                                                    
#>    Poor            │        5.3              5          1.3        61   
#>    Fair            │       22.4             62         15.8       266   
#>    Good            │       49.9            193         49.1       558   
#>    Very good       │       22.4            133         33.8       295   
#>    (Missing)       │                         7                     20   
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Total %    p    Effect size 
#> ───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────
#>  smoking           │          <.001      .14     
#>    No              │  78.8                       
#>    Yes             │  21.2                       
#>    (Missing)       │                             
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  self_rated_health │          <.001      .31     
#>    Poor            │   5.2                       
#>    Fair            │  22.5                       
#>    Good            │  47.3                       
#>    Very good       │  25.0                       
#>    (Missing)       │                             
#> 
#> Note. N = 1200: Lower secondary (n = 261), Upper secondary (n = 539), Tertiary (n = 400). Percentages are column percentages. P-values: Pearson chi-squared test. Cramér's V: smoking. Goodman-Kruskal Gamma: self_rated_health.

smoking keeps its automatic Cramér’s V (.14) while self_rated_health switches from the automatic Tau-b (.20) to Gamma (.31) – Gamma is larger on the same table because it ignores tied pairs. Since the two measures differ, the header collapses to "Effect size" and the note documents the per-row choice.

Add confidence intervals with assoc_ci = TRUE. In the rendered formats (gt, tinytable, flextable, word) the CI is shown inline after the measure, e.g. .14 [.08, .19], under a header that states its level, V [95% CI] (demonstrated in the final section). In the default console table and in the "data.frame", "excel" and "clipboard" outputs, separate columns named 95% CI LL and 95% CI UL are added, as the other tables name their interval columns; in the long format ("long") the bounds fill es_ci_lower / es_ci_upper:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = smoking,
  by = education,
  assoc_ci = TRUE,
  output = "data.frame"
)
#>   variable   label     level     .row_role Lower secondary n Lower secondary %
#> 1  smoking smoking      <NA> factor_header                NA                NA
#> 2  smoking smoking        No         level               179          69.64981
#> 3  smoking smoking       Yes         level                78          30.35019
#> 4  smoking smoking (Missing)       missing                 4                NA
#>   Upper secondary n Upper secondary % Tertiary n Tertiary % Total n  Total %
#> 1                NA                NA         NA         NA      NA       NA
#> 2               415          78.74763        332   84.91049     926 78.80851
#> 3               112          21.25237         59   15.08951     249 21.19149
#> 4                12                NA          9         NA      25       NA
#>              p         V  95% CI LL 95% CI UL
#> 1 2.012877e-05 0.1356677 0.07909264 0.1913716
#> 2           NA        NA         NA        NA
#> 3           NA        NA         NA        NA
#> 4           NA        NA         NA        NA

Chi-squared or Fisher’s exact test

The chi-squared test is an approximation, unreliable when expected counts are small. With test = "auto", the default, each variable takes Pearson’s chi-squared test when every expected count of its table is at least 5, and Fisher’s exact test otherwise: the rule of gtsummary’s add_p(). The note names the test of each variable. In the first 40 respondents, smoking has an expected count of 3.6 and takes the exact test:

table_categorical(
  sochealth[1:40, ],
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
  by = sex
)
#> Categorical table by sex
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Female n  Female %  Male n  Male %  Total n  Total %   p   
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking           │                                                       .258 
#>    No              │    16       72.7      16     88.9     32      80.0         
#>    Yes             │     6       27.3       2     11.1      8      20.0         
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  physical_activity │                                                       .726 
#>    No              │    11       50.0       8     44.4     19      47.5         
#>    Yes             │    11       50.0      10     55.6     21      52.5         
#> 
#>  Variable          │  φ  
#> ───────────────────┼─────
#>  smoking           │ .20 
#>    No              │     
#>    Yes             │     
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌
#>  physical_activity │ .06 
#>    No              │     
#>    Yes             │     
#> 
#> Note. N = 40: Female (n = 22), Male (n = 18). Percentages are column percentages. P-values: Pearson chi-squared test (physical_activity); Fisher exact test (smoking).

test = "chisq" tests every variable by the chi-squared, as before 0.14.0, and test = "fisher" tests every variable exactly. Fisher’s exact test of a table larger than 2x2 is the Freeman-Halton extension. When its exact enumeration fails on a large sparse table, the p-value is its Monte Carlo estimate over simulate_B tables, and the note says so; set a seed to reproduce it. The long output gives the test of each variable in test_type.

A 2x2 table, a two-level variable by two groups, has two more tests. test = "midp" takes the Fisher mid-p test, which counts the tables as probable as the observed one at half their probability: it is less conservative than Fisher’s exact test, and Fagerland, Lydersen and Laake (2017) recommend it at every sample size. test = "n1" takes Campbell’s N-1 chi-squared test when every expected count is at least 1, and Fisher’s exact test otherwise. A larger table keeps the "auto" rule, and the note names the test of each variable:

table_categorical(
  sochealth[1:40, ],
  select = c(smoking, education),
  by = sex,
  test = "midp"
)
#> Categorical table by sex
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Female n  Female %  Male n  Male %  Total n  Total %   p   
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking           │                                                       .184 
#>    No              │    16       72.7      16     88.9     32      80.0         
#>    Yes             │     6       27.3       2     11.1      8      20.0         
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  education         │                                                       .461 
#>    Lower secondary │     6       27.3       2     11.1      8      20.0         
#>    Upper secondary │    10       45.5       9     50.0     19      47.5         
#>    Tertiary        │     6       27.3       7     38.9     13      32.5         
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Effect size 
#> ───────────────────┼─────────────
#>  smoking           │     .20     
#>    No              │             
#>    Yes             │             
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  education         │     .21     
#>    Lower secondary │             
#>    Upper secondary │             
#>    Tertiary        │             
#> 
#> Note. N = 40: Female (n = 22), Male (n = 18). Percentages are column percentages. P-values: Fisher exact test (education); Fisher mid-p test (smoking). Phi: smoking. Cramér's V: education.

Descriptive tables without tests

The test and the association measure are two separate choices: p_value = FALSE removes the test (the p column, and test_type, statistic, df and p.value from the long output), and assoc_measure = "none" removes the measure. Together they give a purely descriptive table, with the same group columns and headers:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
  by = sex,
  p_value = FALSE,
  assoc_measure = "none"
)
#> Categorical table by sex
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Female n  Female %  Male n  Male %  Total n  Total % 
#> ───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking           │                                                      
#>    No              │   475       78.4     451     79.3     926     78.8   
#>    Yes             │   131       21.6     118     20.7     249     21.2   
#>    (Missing)       │    14                 11               25            
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  physical_activity │                                                      
#>    No              │   334       53.9     316     54.5     650     54.2   
#>    Yes             │   286       46.1     264     45.5     550     45.8   
#> 
#> Note. N = 1200: Female (n = 620), Male (n = 580). Percentages are column percentages.

Balance: the standardized mean difference

For a baseline table read as a balance check rather than a significance test, smd = TRUE adds the standardized mean difference between the two groups of by, on the variable row beside p:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, self_rated_health),
  by = sex,
  smd = TRUE
)
#> Categorical table by sex
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Female n  Female %  Male n  Male %  Total n  Total %   p   
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking           │                                                       .713 
#>    No              │   475       78.4     451     79.3     926     78.8         
#>    Yes             │   131       21.6     118     20.7     249     21.2         
#>    (Missing)       │    14                 11               25                  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  self_rated_health │                                                       .849 
#>    Poor            │    31        5.1      30      5.3      61      5.2         
#>    Fair            │   143       23.4     123     21.6     266     22.5         
#>    Good            │   282       46.2     276     48.4     558     47.3         
#>    Very good       │   154       25.2     141     24.7     295     25.0         
#>    (Missing)       │    10                 10               20                  
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Effect size  SMD  
#> ───────────────────┼───────────────────
#>  smoking           │     .01      0.02 
#>    No              │                   
#>    Yes             │                   
#>    (Missing)       │                   
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  self_rated_health │     .03      0.05 
#>    Poor            │                   
#>    Fair            │                   
#>    Good            │                   
#>    Very good       │                   
#>    (Missing)       │                   
#> 
#> Note. N = 1200: Female (n = 620), Male (n = 580). Percentages are column percentages. P-values: Pearson chi-squared test. Phi: smoking. Cramér's V: self_rated_health. SMD direction: Female − Male. The usual imbalance threshold is |SMD| > 0.1. For a variable with more than two categories the SMD is the multivariate (Mahalanobis) distance between the two profiles of proportions, and is therefore unsigned. SMD = standardized mean difference.

Two categories give the Bernoulli form, signed, group 1 minus group 2 in the order the table displays them. Three or more give the multivariate (Mahalanobis) distance between the two profiles of proportions: a distance, so it has no sign and no upper bound of 1 — the table note says so whenever such a variable is present, and the "long" output names the kernel each row took in smd_type.

Exactly two groups are required, as in table_continuous(). The "(Missing)" level of drop_na = FALSE is displayed and never enters the diagnostic. There is no confidence interval and no p-value on this column by design. Under weights the profiles are the weighted proportions, and because a profile of proportions is unchanged by a global rescaling of the weights, rescale cannot move this column.

A balance table usually shows no test: p_value = FALSE removes the categorical p column as table_continuous(p_value = FALSE) removes its own, so a mixed balance table can drop both. When the p column stays, it can be adjusted: p_adjust = "holm" (or "BH") adjusts the tests of all the variables together, and the note says so.

Weighted tables

Pass survey weights with the weights argument. By default (rescale = FALSE) the weights are used as-is; rescale = TRUE rescales them so the total weighted N equals the number of observations (here 1200, against a raw weight sum of 1196.474). Displayed counts are weighted counts rounded to integers at display time – the SPSS Crosstabs convention – while the machine formats ("data.frame", "long") carry the exact fractional weighted counts:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
  by = education,
  weights = "weight",
  rescale = TRUE
)
#> Categorical table by education

#>    Yes             │         85               32.8                231

#>  smoking           │                                                    
#>    No              │       78.5            325         84.4       919

Handling missing values

By default, missing values are displayed as a “(Missing)” category (drop_na = FALSE), with their count and no percentage: the percentages are computed on the observed values. percent_base = "total" puts the missing values back in the base, the percentages then summing over every observation, as before 0.14.0. Set drop_na = TRUE to remove them. The removal happens before each cross-tabulation, variable by variable: each row variable keeps its own complete cases (on itself and on by), so the count of a variable can differ from the N of the note and across variables within the same table – this is available-case analysis per cross-table, not listwise deletion over the whole selection. The removal is disclosed in a table note rather than silent:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = income_group,
  by = education,
  drop_na = TRUE
)
#> Categorical table by education
#> 
#>  Variable       │ Lower secondary n  Lower secondary %  Upper secondary n 
#> ────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  income_group   │                                                         
#>    Low          │        87                33.7                115        
#>    Lower middle │        92                35.7                186        
#>    Upper middle │        58                22.5                135        
#>    High         │        21                 8.1                 94        
#> 
#>  Variable       │ Upper secondary %  Tertiary n  Tertiary %  Total n  Total % 
#> ────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  income_group   │                                                             
#>    Low          │       21.7             45         11.4       247     20.9   
#>    Lower middle │       35.1            110         27.9       388     32.8   
#>    Upper middle │       25.5            135         34.3       328     27.7   
#>    High         │       17.7            104         26.4       219     18.5   
#> 
#>  Variable       │   p    τb  
#> ────────────────┼────────────
#>  income_group   │ <.001  .22 
#>    Low          │            
#>    Lower middle │            
#>    Upper middle │            
#>    High         │            
#> 
#> Note. N = 1200: Lower secondary (n = 261), Upper secondary (n = 539), Tertiary (n = 400). Percentages are column percentages. Missing values removed: income_group (18). P-value: Pearson chi-squared test.

With several selected variables the note lists each variable’s removals separately: selecting smoking and physical_activity together under drop_na = TRUE keeps 1175 and 1200 complete cases respectively, in the same table.

A level of your data that already reads “(Missing)” would sit beside that category under the same label, and a level of by named “Total” beside the margin. The table then stops with an error that gives the two ways out: rename the level, or give the category another label with options(spicy.labels = list(row_missing_level = "(Not stated)")) (the margin’s key is header_margin_total).

Filtering and reordering levels

Use levels_keep to display only specific levels. The order you specify controls the display order, which is useful for placing “(Missing)” first to highlight missingness:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = income_group,
  by = education,
  drop_na = FALSE,
  levels_keep = c("(Missing)", "Low", "High")
)
#> Categorical table by education
#> 
#>  Variable     │ Lower secondary n  Lower secondary %  Upper secondary n 
#> ──────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  income_group │                                                         
#>    (Missing)  │         3                                      9        
#>    Low        │        87                33.7                115        
#>    High       │        21                 8.1                 94        
#> 
#>  Variable     │ Upper secondary %  Tertiary n  Tertiary %  Total n  Total % 
#> ──────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  income_group │                                                             
#>    (Missing)  │                         6                     18            
#>    Low        │       21.7             45         11.4       247     20.9   
#>    High       │       17.7            104         26.4       219     18.5   
#> 
#>  Variable     │   p    τb  
#> ──────────────┼────────────
#>  income_group │ <.001  .22 
#>    (Missing)  │            
#>    Low        │            
#>    High       │            
#> 
#> Note. N = 1200: Lower secondary (n = 261), Upper secondary (n = 539), Tertiary (n = 400). Percentages are column percentages. P-value: Pearson chi-squared test.

levels_keep filters the display only: counts, percentages, the chi-squared test, and the association measure are all still computed on the full cross-table. That is why the displayed percentages no longer sum to 100 (within “Lower secondary”: 33.7 + 8.1 = 41.8 – the hidden “Lower middle” and “Upper middle” levels still count in the denominator), and why p and Tau-b are identical to the unfiltered table. To recompute the statistics on a subset of levels, filter the data before calling table_categorical().

Formatting options

Control the number of digits for percentages, p-values, and the association measure:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = smoking,
  by = education,
  percent_digits = 2,
  p_digits = 4,
  effect_size_digits = 3
)
#> Categorical table by education
#> 
#>  Variable    │ Lower secondary n  Lower secondary %  Upper secondary n 
#> ─────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking     │                                                         
#>    No        │        179               69.65               415        
#>    Yes       │         78               30.35               112        
#>    (Missing) │          4                                    12        
#> 
#>  Variable    │ Upper secondary %  Tertiary n  Tertiary %  Total n  Total % 
#> ─────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  smoking     │                                                             
#>    No        │       78.75           332        84.91       926     78.81  
#>    Yes       │       21.25            59        15.09       249     21.19  
#>    (Missing) │                         9                     25            
#> 
#>  Variable    │   p      V   
#> ─────────────┼──────────────
#>  smoking     │ <.0001  .136 
#>    No        │              
#>    Yes       │              
#>    (Missing) │              
#> 
#> Note. N = 1200: Lower secondary (n = 261), Upper secondary (n = 539), Tertiary (n = 400). Percentages are column percentages. P-value: Pearson chi-squared test. V = Cramér's V.

p_digits drives both the displayed precision of the p column and the small-p threshold (p_digits = 3 -> <.001, p_digits = 4 -> <.0001), matching table_continuous() and table_continuous_lm().

Decimal alignment

By default (align = "decimal") numeric columns are aligned on the decimal mark, the standard scientific-publication convention (SPSS, SAS, LaTeX siunitx). Numeric cells are pre-padded with figure-spaces (U+2007, spaces exactly one digit wide) so that every string in a column has the same width with the decimal mark at the same internal position; centering those uniform-width strings then stacks the decimal points vertically. The same pad-then-center strategy is applied on every rendering engine (gt, tinytable, flextable, word, ASCII print) for a homogeneous rendering – same single-font policy as table_regression(). The clipboard is the exception: its payload is delimited text meant to be parsed, and a padded number would paste as text next to an unpadded number, so its cells travel unpadded. The native gt::cols_align_decimal() and tinytable::style_tt(align = "d") primitives are deliberately not used: the former renders visually right-aligned and the latter centers each cell on its own value rather than on the decimal mark, which would be inconsistent with the other engines.

"center" and "right" apply literal alignment:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
  by = sex,
  align = "right"
)
#> Categorical table by sex
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Female n  Female %  Male n  Male %  Total n  Total %     p

Tidying for downstream pipelines

table_categorical() returns an object that can be coerced to a plain data.frame / tbl_df (the displayed table, as with output = "data.frame") or piped into broom::tidy() / broom::glance() for any downstream tidyverse-stats workflow:

out <- table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
  by = sex
)

# One row per (variable x level x group) with broom-style columns
# (variable, label, level, .row_role, group, .group_role, total, n,
# proportion): the column name and the label displayed. The Total
# margin is flagged by `total`; filter it out with `!total` to count
# each observation once.
broom::tidy(out)
#> # A tibble: 15 × 9
#>    variable       label level .row_role group .group_role total     n proportion
#>    <chr>          <chr> <chr> <chr>     <chr> <chr>       <lgl> <int>      <dbl>
#>  1 smoking        smok… No    level     Fema… group       FALSE   475      0.784
#>  2 smoking        smok… No    level     Male  group       FALSE   451      0.793
#>  3 smoking        smok… No    level     Total total       TRUE    926      0.788
#>  4 smoking        smok… Yes   level     Fema… group       FALSE   131      0.216
#>  5 smoking        smok… Yes   level     Male  group       FALSE   118      0.207
#>  6 smoking        smok… Yes   level     Total total       TRUE    249      0.212
#>  7 smoking        smok… (Mis… missing   Fema… group       FALSE    14     NA    
#>  8 smoking        smok… (Mis… missing   Male  group       FALSE    11     NA    
#>  9 smoking        smok… (Mis… missing   Total total       TRUE     25     NA    
#> 10 physical_acti… phys… No    level     Fema… group       FALSE   334      0.539
#> 11 physical_acti… phys… No    level     Male  group       FALSE   316      0.545
#> 12 physical_acti… phys… No    level     Total total       TRUE    650      0.542
#> 13 physical_acti… phys… Yes   level     Fema… group       FALSE   286      0.461

Multiple-response items

A “check all that apply” question is a set of yes/no items answered by the same respondents, like the five info_* items of sochealth, the sources of health information used in the past 12 months. It is not one categorical variable: the choices outnumber the respondents, and the chi-squared test of the items-by-groups table is not valid. table_multiresponse() reads the items as one question, with its own bases, percentages, and tests, as Multiple-response questions explains.

Rendered outputs and export

The rendered formats produce publication-ready tables for HTML and Word workflows. The "gt" format produces a table with APA-style borders, column spanners, and decimal alignment:

pkgdown_dark_gt(
  table_categorical(
    sochealth,
    select = c(smoking, physical_activity, dentist_12m),
    by = education,
    output = "gt"
  )
)

The "tinytable" format applies the same layout conventions through the lightweight tinytable engine (here a two-group table by sex):

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
  by = sex,
  output = "tinytable"
)

With assoc_ci = TRUE, the rendered formats show the confidence interval inline after the association measure:

pkgdown_dark_gt(
  table_categorical(
    sochealth,
    select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
    by = education,
    assoc_ci = TRUE,
    output = "gt"
  )
)

For Excel export, provide a file path:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity, dentist_12m),
  by = education,
  output = "excel",
  excel_path = "my_table.xlsx"
)

For Word, use output = "word":

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity, dentist_12m),
  by = education,
  output = "word",
  word_path = "my_table.docx"
)

You can also copy directly to the clipboard for pasting into a spreadsheet or a text editor:

table_categorical(
  sochealth,
  select = c(smoking, physical_activity),
  by = education,
  output = "clipboard"
)
